content.text:
Lighthouses are among the oldest deliberate works of navigation, and their history follows the history of the sea itself: the need to bring ships safely past dangerous coasts, and the steady growth of the knowledge needed to do so. The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbour around 280 BCE, in the reign of Ptolemy II. It was designed by the architect Sostratus of Cnidus, and ancient accounts put its height at somewhere near 100 metres, which would have made it one of the tallest structures in the world for many centuries. A fire burned at its summit, and the light was thought to be visible far out to sea. The Pharos survived for more than a millennium before earthquakes weakened it, and its ruins were finally lost in the early fourteenth century. Its name proved more durable than the building. In Greek, Latin and many modern languages the word for a lighthouse descends from it, as in the Italian *faro*, the French *phare* and the Portuguese *farol*.

The Romans built a number of coastal towers, and a few have survived into the modern era. The best known is the Tower of Hercules at A Coruña in north-west Spain, probably dating from the late first or early second century CE. It is the oldest lighthouse still in use, and it has been restored several times, most recently in the eighteenth century, when its outer casing was rebuilt. Other Roman towers, at Dover and elsewhere along the Channel and the North Sea, served as signal stations or watch towers as much as navigational aids. After the fall of the western empire, the knowledge needed to build such structures became scarce in much of Europe, and for several centuries the guidance of ships relied largely on local knowledge, church bells, and fires lit on headlands or on towers that were built for other purposes. Some medieval harbour towns maintained beacons, and religious houses sometimes kept lights to guide travellers across dangerous crossings, but there was no systematic network.

The modern lighthouse emerged in the early modern period, driven by the growth of maritime trade and the expansion of naval power. The Tour de Cordouan at the mouth of the Gironde in France was begun in 1584 and completed in 1611, and its design, with a richly decorated tower and a lantern at the top, was intended partly as a statement of royal prestige. In Britain the Corporation of Trinity House, chartered by Henry VIII in 1514, gradually took responsibility for marking the coasts, and by the seventeenth century the problem of lighting the most dangerous rocks had become pressing. The Eddystone Rock, some fourteen kilometres off Plymouth, was a notorious hazard, and in 1698 Henry Winstanley built the first lighthouse there on a wooden framework bolted to the rock. Winstanley was a showman and an inventor as well as an engineer, and he was fond of tinkering with his own structure. In November 1703 the Great Storm destroyed the tower, and Winstanley died in it, having gone out to check on its repairs.

The next attempts were more durable. John Rudyerd replaced the wooden structure in 1706 with a tower of timber and stone, which stood for nearly fifty years. Its successor, designed by John Smeaton and completed in 1759, was the most influential structure of its age. Smeaton studied the properties of hydraulic lime, which sets under water, and he shaped the granite blocks so that they interlocked in a form that he compared to the trunk of an oak tree. His tower established principles of construction that engineers relied on for generations, and it stood until the rock beneath it began to erode in the 1870s. The tower was then dismantled and the top portion was re-erected on Plymouth Hoe as a monument. A new lighthouse was built on the rock by James Douglass, and it remains in service today.

Scotland produced an equally remarkable achievement at the Bell Rock, a submerged reef off the coast of Angus that is covered at high tide. Robert Stevenson, a member of the family whose descendants would later include Robert Louis Stevenson, spent years designing and building a tower there between 1807 and 1810. The work was carried out by men who lived in a floating barracks and could only labour during the short windows of low tide. The completed light, first shone in 1811, is still operating, and it stands as a monument to the careful and often dangerous labour that lay behind so many of these structures.

The most significant advance in the technology of the light itself came from France. Before the nineteenth century, lights were typically open fires, then oil lamps with reflectors that threw their output in a fairly diffuse pattern. In 1822 the physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel presented a design for a lens made of concentric rings of glass prisms, which could bend almost all the light from a lamp into a narrow horizontal beam. The lens could be made large and yet remain relatively light, and it allowed a lamp of modest power to be seen from many miles away. The first Fresnel lens was installed at Cordouan in 1823, and the design was rapidly adopted across Europe and the Americas. Lenses were graded by size, with first-order lenses, the largest, being placed on the most important coasts. Some are still in use, though most have now been replaced by modern optics.

Keeping the lights burning was itself a demanding task. Keepers climbed the towers to trim wicks, clean glass, wind clockwork mechanisms that rotated the lenses, and log the weather and the state of the light. Isolated stations were lonely and dangerous, and the keepers faced both the sea and the boredom of long postings with few visitors. The Flannan Isles light in the Outer Hebrides became famous in 1900, when three keepers vanished from the island in December. The relief boat found the lamp still lit and the keepers' meal half prepared, but no trace of the men was ever found, and the disappearance has never been fully explained.

The twentieth century transformed lighthouse keeping. Electricity replaced oil, and the Swedish engineer Gustaf Dalén invented the AGA sun valve in 1912, a device that automatically switched lights on at dusk and off at dawn, for which he received the Nobel Prize in Physics that year. Automatic lights, radio beacons, and later satellite navigation made the task of guiding ships increasingly independent of the keeper on the rock. Many stations were automated, and the last manned lighthouse in the United States, on Ilwaco in Washington State, was closed to keepers in 1990. Today most lighthouses operate without staff, monitored remotely, and many have been turned into museums, hotels, or sites of local heritage.

The lighthouse thus has a longer history than almost any other engineered structure still in use. It began as a symbol of royal power and commercial ambition, passed through the hands of engineers who learned to build in the open sea, and was transformed by optical physics and then by electrical and automatic control. Its form has changed dramatically, but its purpose has stayed the same: to tell a navigator where the land is, and where the danger lies.
